items.definition: An attack on the person instead of on the claim.
items.example: You did not read the report, so your opinion does not count is an ad hominem.

items.definition: The turning of an answer into an answer about somebody else.
items.example: You did the same thing last year is whataboutism: it answers nothing.

items.definition: The formal name for whataboutism; it means "you too".
items.example: The reply was a tu quoque: it pointed at the other person's record and stayed there.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.

items.definition: The choice of words around a fact, which changes how the fact feels.
items.example: The framing changed nothing: 400 a month is the same money as 4,800 a year.

items.definition: A reply that takes the point that was made and answers it with a reason.
items.example: The rebuttal gave the reason and asked for the same test on the other side.

items.definition: A repeated attack on a person's memory and judgement, so that they stop trusting what they remember.
items.example: It was gaslighting: she was told her own account of the meeting was wrong.

items.definition: The person who denies the shared account and attacks the person who holds it; the word names the act, not the character.
items.example: The gaslighter kept the denial flat and turned the talk to her character.

items.definition: What two people agree happened, and what each of them remembers about it.
items.example: Their shared account of the shift was simple, and both of them could still say it.

items.definition: Keeping the account but changing the words in it, until the meaning that was shared is gone.
items.example: The word was changed from late to careless, and that was revisionism.

items.definition: The doubt a person is given about their own memory, until they check themselves instead of the facts.
items.example: The result was manufactured doubt: he began to check his own memory instead of the record.

items.definition: The name of the pattern of three moves: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.
items.example: The pattern was DARVO: deny, attack, and reverse victim and offender.

items.definition: The refusal to accept a shared account, said in a way that does not change when the evidence appears.
items.example: The denial was said the same way every time, and the message did not change it.

items.definition: The move that turns on the person who holds the account, so that the person becomes the problem.
items.example: The attack moved the talk from the handover to her tone.

items.definition: The move that puts the two sides in the wrong places, crediting the harm to the person who suffered it.
items.example: The reversal put the person who caused the harm in the place of the person who suffered it.

items.definition: Turning a question back on the person who asked it, so that the original question is never answered.
items.example: The deflection worked once, and I still had not answered what was wrong with the drawing.

items.definition: Putting your own act on the other person, and calling it the other person's character.
items.example: It was projection: the person who had been aggressive called the other one aggressive.

items.definition: Bringing a third person into a dispute between two, so that the two cannot settle it themselves.
items.example: Triangulation brought a third person into a dispute between two people.

items.definition: The written record that keeps a shared account alive when memory is attacked.
items.example: The documentation was a handover note, a date and a message.

items.definition: The small set of fixed sentences used to rewrite an account, at work and at home.
items.example: The gaslighting vocabulary is short: you are misremembering, I never said that.

items.definition: One only; not multiple.
items.example: A single file is a gallery of one.

items.definition: The situation of being without a romantic partner, seen as a general condition rather than one person's story.
items.example: Long-term singleness has its own vocabulary, and its own pressures.

items.definition: Describing a person who has no romantic partner, without saying whether that is a choice.
items.example: He said he was unpartnered, and he said it without any apology in his voice.

items.definition: The repeated sense that a status such as being single is a condition to be explained, corrected or ended.
items.example: The social pressure arrives in small questions, not in one cruel remark.

items.definition: A mark of disgrace that a group attaches to a status, so that the status itself becomes hard to show.
items.example: In some offices there is a stigma against a long single life, and in others there is none.

items.definition: A settled sense that a situation is acceptable, without the need for it to be improved first.
items.example: Her contentment with the arrangement was visible in the way she answered people.

items.definition: Describing a person who has a romantic relationship, whether or not they live with the other person.
items.example: She is partnered, and her partner works in another city.

items.definition: To live with a partner in the same home without being married to that person.
items.example: They have cohabited for three years and still keep two homes.

items.definition: Describing a person whose marriage has ended legally.
items.example: He is divorced, and the children spend the week with him.

items.definition: Describing a person whose spouse has died.
items.example: She is widowed, and she still keeps the shared photographs on the wall.

items.definition: Describing an ending in which the two people settle the practical matters and stay on speaking terms.
items.example: The separation was amicable, so the flat was sold without a lawyer's fight.

items.definition: Being single because that is the arrangement the person has chosen.
items.example: He calls it voluntary singleness, and he means it as a decision rather than a consolation.

items.definition: Being single because the wish for a partner has not been met, rather than by choice.
items.example: She calls it involuntary singleness, and she has stopped apologising for it.

items.definition: The state of being open to a relationship and willing to say yes to the right one.
items.example: His romantic availability changed when he moved to another city, and he says so openly.

items.definition: A metaphor for the meeting of people who are looking for a partner.
items.example: They talked about the dating market for an hour without saying anything about either of them.

items.definition: The group of people who are available to be chosen, counted as a group and not as individuals.
items.example: The supply was small where she lived, and the same people kept appearing.

items.definition: The group of wishes that the people looking are trying to satisfy.
items.example: The demand was for somebody who wanted a quiet life, and that changed who she met.

items.definition: The treatment of a person as a product that can be valued and exchanged.
items.example: The whole conversation turned her into a commodity, and she left the table.

items.definition: Acting in a planned way to produce a result, rather than acting in the way that comes naturally.
items.example: Strategic behaviour won him the interview; it did not make him better at the work.

items.definition: The number the market metaphor assigns to a person, as if it could be measured and compared.
items.example: He talked about his mate value instead of asking what she wanted.
